name: Switchyard
description: Switchyard lets LLM applications route traffic across models and providers while preserving native OpenAI and Anthropic API compatibility - enabling flexible model selection, benchmarking, and cost/performance optimization.

# NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard

Switchyard is an open-source library that helps an AI agent choose which model handles each request. It combines efficient models with more capable models so you can balance task success, cost, and latency on your workload. Adopt Switchyard by embedding its Rust core, **libsy**, in your gateway or agent harness. You own the model clients, credentials, and service. Switchyard supplies the routing decision.

Quickstart  ·  Documentation  ·  Benchmarks  ·  What’s new  ·  Roadmap  ·  Releases  ·  Contributing

## How it works 1. Configure the models an agent can use and choose a routing algorithm. 2. The algorithm examines the request or the agent's recent tool activity. Some algorithms call a model to judge the task. 3. A gateway or agent sends the request to the selected model. Routing can change as the agent continues its work. Evaluate the complete agent, model pool, and routing configuration against your single-model baseline. A cheaper model call does not guarantee a cheaper successfully completed task. The [tuning loop](docs/tuning/index.md) gives the steps for that evaluation, and [Troubleshooting](docs/operations/troubleshooting.md) lists the settings that disable routing without an error. ## How to use it - **[Through an existing gateway](#through-an-existing-gateway):** Use an available gateway integration. - **[Embed libsy in your harness](#embed-libsy-in-your-harness):** Add libsy to a service you operate. - **[Evaluate Switchyard locally](#evaluate-switchyard-locally):** Compare routing configurations with your own model pool using the demo server. ### Through an existing gateway | Gateway | Start here | Deployment and limits | | --- | --- | --- | | **OpenRouter** | [Use Switchyard through OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai/docs/guides/routing/routers/switchyard-router) | Hosted by OpenRouter. Set `model` to `nvidia/switchyard` in API requests. | | **LiteLLM** | [Run the Switchyard routing-plugin example](examples/litellm/README.md#quick-start-with-the-local-proxy) | Experimental and checkout-only. The example pins LiteLLM 1.102.0 and supports Stage routing based on request history, plus Random routing. It cannot service intermediate model calls required by classifier or escalation algorithms. | | **NeMo Relay** | [Build and configure the native plugin](crates/switchyard-nemo-relay-plugin/README.md#build-from-source) | Requires Relay `>=0.10.0, <1.0.0`. The source-build path requires a Rust toolchain and Python 3. | Relay 0.8.x and 0.9.0 can lose upstream error status and details when the plugin is enabled, even for models outside its routes. Review the [upstream error compatibility note](docs/integrations/nemo_relay.md#upstream-error-compatibility) before enabling the plugin. LiteLLM and NeMo Relay run in your own deployment. Follow each gateway's guidance for credentials and service operation. ### Embed libsy in your harness `Algorithm::run_stream` hands model calls and the final routing outcome back to your application. In this development-API outline, comments mark the work your code supplies: ```rust let mut steps = algorithm.run_stream(request, models, state); while let Some(step) = steps.next().await { match step? { Step::CallModel(call) => { // Send call.request through your LLM client. // Give the call future to call.respond(...).await. } Step::CallDecision(call) => { // Send call.request through your decision-model client. // Give its typed response future to call.respond(...).await. } Step::Done(outcome) => { match outcome.response { Some(response) => { // Return this answer; no final LLM call is needed. } None => { // Send outcome.request through your client for the final answer, // or pass it to your gateway to make that call later. } } } } } ``` - **Inputs:** supply an algorithm, model pool, request, and state. - **Calls:** your clients handle model calls. Stage returns a selection; other algorithms may return an answer. - **Start here:** [Rust quickstart](docs/getting_started.md) · [Python bindings](docs/reference/host_integration.md#python-bindings). ### Evaluate Switchyard locally The standalone server is provided only for demos and local evaluation. It is not a supported production deployment path. [Evaluate routing locally](docs/operations/local_evaluation.md) with the standalone server and your own model pool, then [verify routing is active](docs/operations/local_evaluation.md#verify-routing-is-active). The experimental [desktop and terminal quickstart](experimental/switchyard-desktop/README.md) covers local installation, coding-tool connections, sessions, usage, recovery, and uninstall. Agent-specific guides are available for [pi](docs/integrations/pi.md) and [Oh My Pi](docs/integrations/oh_my_pi.md). ## Routing algorithms Start with Auto. Choose Task, Execution, or Composite when you need more control. These names describe routing choices. The configuration keys are unchanged. | Choice | How it chooses | TOML configuration | | --- | --- | --- | | **[Auto](docs/routing_algorithms/overview.md#auto)** | Uses the current default: Execution (Stage), efficient-first, with a confidence threshold of 0.5 and no classifier call. | `type = "auto"` | | **[Task](docs/routing_algorithms/llm_classifier_routing.md)** | A model judges whether the efficient model can handle the task. | `type = "llm_classifier"`, `mode = "capability"` | | **[Execution](docs/routing_algorithms/stage_router_routing.md)** | Uses recent tool activity and outcome signals to choose a model as the agent runs. | `type = "stage_router"` | | **[Composite](docs/routing_algorithms/composite_routing.md)** | Combines Task and Execution: a classifier sets the default model tier when execution signals are uncertain. | `type = "composite"` | Auto is a fixed preset in v0.3.0. It does not compare strategies at runtime. The TOML runner supports `type = "auto"`. In Rust, use `StageRouterConfig::new(PickerMode::EfficientFirst, 0.5)` for the same preset. The [routing overview](docs/routing_algorithms/overview.md) lists all strategies, including the [Plan/Execute configuration for Stage](docs/routing_algorithms/stage_router_routing.md#plan-and-execute), [escalation](docs/routing_algorithms/escalation_router_routing.md), [advisor](docs/routing_algorithms/advisor_gate_routing.md), [sub-agent](docs/routing_algorithms/subagent_routing.md), and [random](docs/routing_algorithms/random_routing.md). Integration support varies: check the gateway guide before choosing an algorithm. [Prefill routing](docs/routing_algorithms/prefill_routing.md) is designed for fast, efficient model selection using a model's prefill activations and a classifier trained on your own evaluation data. ## Evaluation and reference [Compare benchmark results and configs](docs/benchmarks.md) for Terminal-Bench 2.1 and DeepSWE. For latency and routing overhead testing, see [Soak Testing](docs/operations/soak_test.md). ### Further reading - [Benchmark setup and profiles](benchmark/README.md): run your own baseline and routing comparisons. - [Mechanics of Libsy](docs/mechanics_of_libsy.md): steps, model calls, and routing outcomes. - [TOML schema](docs/reference/toml_schema.md): configuration fields and defaults. - [Rust crate reference](docs/reference/rust_api.md): core and optional integration crates. - [Installation](INSTALLATION.md): package and platform requirements. ## Components Pre-1.0 software. APIs, configuration, and routing behavior can change between releases. Pin the version you integrate. | Component | Stability | Use it for | Guidance | |---|---|---|---| | `switchyard-libsy` | **Beta** | Routing embedded in your own gateway or harness. You own model calls, credentials, and retries. | Trial integrations. API will change before v1.0. | | `switchyard-llm-client` | **Alpha** | HTTP model calls and protocol translation alongside libsy. | Experiments and pilots. | | `switchyard-runner` | **Alpha** | Running configured routes inside another runtime, such as NeMo Relay. | Integration work and supervised pilots. | | `switchyard-server` | **Demo** | A standalone OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible proxy. | Demos and local evaluation only; not a supported production path. | ## What’s new Features and integrations recently merged into `main`. - **2026-10-16 · Route between Sonnet and Opus in Claude Code**\ Use your Claude login for automatic routing on Linux x86_64 and see the selected model in the status line. [Setup guide →](examples/claude/README.md) - **2026-10-15 · Use decision models in composite routing**\ Use Mercury Decide to judge tasks and Stage routing to adjust model selection as tools run. [Example configuration →](dev-server/config.toml) - **2026-10-13 · Use Jev to choose between models**\ Configure Jev as a task judge with candidate descriptions and a probability cutoff. [Configuration guide →](docs/routing_algorithms/composite_routing.md#decision-model-classifier) - **2026-10-12 · Bring Switchyard to TypeScript and Pi**\ Select models in Node.js or try automatic routing through Pi’s virtual models. [TypeScript bindings →](bindings/typescript/README.md) · [Pi example →](examples/pi/README.md) ## Community and license [Report an issue](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Switchyard/issues) · [Contribute](CONTRIBUTING.md) · [Code of conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md) [Apache 2.0](LICENSE). Copyright NVIDIA Corporation.

NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard

Switchyard is an open-source library that helps an AI agent choose which model handles each request. It combines efficient models with more capable models so you can balance task success, cost, and latency on your workload.

Adopt Switchyard by embedding its Rust core, libsy, in your gateway or agent harness. You own the model clients, credentials, and service. Switchyard supplies the routing decision.

Quickstart  ·  Documentation  ·  Benchmarks  ·  What’s new  ·  Roadmap  ·  Releases  ·  Contributing

How it works

  1. Configure the models an agent can use and choose a routing algorithm.
  2. The algorithm examines the request or the agent's recent tool activity. Some algorithms call a model to judge the task.
  3. A gateway or agent sends the request to the selected model. Routing can change as the agent continues its work.

Evaluate the complete agent, model pool, and routing configuration against your single-model baseline. A cheaper model call does not guarantee a cheaper successfully completed task. The tuning loop gives the steps for that evaluation, and Troubleshooting lists the settings that disable routing without an error.

How to use it

  • Through an existing gateway: Use an available gateway integration.
  • Embed libsy in your harness: Add libsy to a service you operate.
  • Evaluate Switchyard locally: Compare routing configurations with your own model pool using the demo server.

Through an existing gateway

Gateway Start here Deployment and limits
OpenRouter Use Switchyard through OpenRouter Hosted by OpenRouter. Set model to nvidia/switchyard in API requests.
LiteLLM Run the Switchyard routing-plugin example Experimental and checkout-only. The example pins LiteLLM 1.102.0 and supports Stage routing based on request history, plus Random routing. It cannot service intermediate model calls required by classifier or escalation algorithms.
NeMo Relay Build and configure the native plugin Requires Relay >=0.10.0, <1.0.0. The source-build path requires a Rust toolchain and Python 3.

Relay 0.8.x and 0.9.0 can lose upstream error status and details when the plugin is enabled, even for models outside its routes. Review the upstream error compatibility note before enabling the plugin.

LiteLLM and NeMo Relay run in your own deployment. Follow each gateway's guidance for credentials and service operation.

Embed libsy in your harness

Algorithm::run_stream hands model calls and the final routing outcome back to your application. In this development-API outline, comments mark the work your code supplies:

let mut steps = algorithm.run_stream(request, models, state);
while let Some(step) = steps.next().await {
    match step? {
        Step::CallModel(call) => {
            // Send call.request through your LLM client.
            // Give the call future to call.respond(...).await.
        }
        Step::CallDecision(call) => {
            // Send call.request through your decision-model client.
            // Give its typed response future to call.respond(...).await.
        }
        Step::Done(outcome) => {
            match outcome.response {
                Some(response) => {
                    // Return this answer; no final LLM call is needed.
                }
                None => {
                    // Send outcome.request through your client for the final answer,
                    // or pass it to your gateway to make that call later.
                }
            }
        }
    }
}
  • Inputs: supply an algorithm, model pool, request, and state.
  • Calls: your clients handle model calls. Stage returns a selection; other algorithms may return an answer.
  • Start here: Rust quickstart · Python bindings.

Evaluate Switchyard locally

The standalone server is provided only for demos and local evaluation. It is not a supported production deployment path.

Evaluate routing locally with the standalone server and your own model pool, then verify routing is active.

The experimental desktop and terminal quickstart covers local installation, coding-tool connections, sessions, usage, recovery, and uninstall.

Agent-specific guides are available for pi and Oh My Pi.

Routing algorithms

Start with Auto. Choose Task, Execution, or Composite when you need more control. These names describe routing choices. The configuration keys are unchanged.

Choice How it chooses TOML configuration
Auto Uses the current default: Execution (Stage), efficient-first, with a confidence threshold of 0.5 and no classifier call. type = "auto"
Task A model judges whether the efficient model can handle the task. type = "llm_classifier", mode = "capability"
Execution Uses recent tool activity and outcome signals to choose a model as the agent runs. type = "stage_router"
Composite Combines Task and Execution: a classifier sets the default model tier when execution signals are uncertain. type = "composite"

Auto is a fixed preset in v0.3.0. It does not compare strategies at runtime. The TOML runner supports type = "auto". In Rust, use StageRouterConfig::new(PickerMode::EfficientFirst, 0.5) for the same preset.

The routing overview lists all strategies, including the Plan/Execute configuration for Stage, escalation, advisor, sub-agent, and random. Integration support varies: check the gateway guide before choosing an algorithm.

Prefill routing is designed for fast, efficient model selection using a model's prefill activations and a classifier trained on your own evaluation data.

Evaluation and reference

Compare benchmark results and configs for Terminal-Bench 2.1 and DeepSWE. For latency and routing overhead testing, see Soak Testing.

Further reading

  • Benchmark setup and profiles: run your own baseline and routing comparisons.
  • Mechanics of Libsy: steps, model calls, and routing outcomes.
  • TOML schema: configuration fields and defaults.
  • Rust crate reference: core and optional integration crates.
  • Installation: package and platform requirements.

Components

Pre-1.0 software. APIs, configuration, and routing behavior can change between releases. Pin the version you integrate.

Component Stability Use it for Guidance
switchyard-libsy Beta Routing embedded in your own gateway or harness. You own model calls, credentials, and retries. Trial integrations. API will change before v1.0.
switchyard-llm-client Alpha HTTP model calls and protocol translation alongside libsy. Experiments and pilots.
switchyard-runner Alpha Running configured routes inside another runtime, such as NeMo Relay. Integration work and supervised pilots.
switchyard-server Demo A standalone OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible proxy. Demos and local evaluation only; not a supported production path.

What’s new

Features and integrations recently merged into main.

  • 2026-10-16 · Route between Sonnet and Opus in Claude Code
    Use your Claude login for automatic routing on Linux x86_64 and see the selected model in the status line. Setup guide →

  • 2026-10-15 · Use decision models in composite routing
    Use Mercury Decide to judge tasks and Stage routing to adjust model selection as tools run. Example configuration →

  • 2026-10-13 · Use Jev to choose between models
    Configure Jev as a task judge with candidate descriptions and a probability cutoff. Configuration guide →

  • 2026-10-12 · Bring Switchyard to TypeScript and Pi
    Select models in Node.js or try automatic routing through Pi’s virtual models. TypeScript bindings → · Pi example →

Community and license

Report an issue · Contribute · Code of conduct

releases.name: v0.3.0
releases.body:
# Switchyard v0.3.0

Switchyard 0.3.0 adds reusable runner integrations, Advisor Gate and Composite routing, Auto presets, and updated Rust and Python embedding APIs. It also fixes provider translation and tool-loop behavior and removes the legacy Python server and coding-agent launchers.

This is a breaking upgrade for library and Python CLI users. Review the migration notes below before upgrading.

[Full changelog](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Switchyard/blob/v0.3.0/CHANGELOG.md#030) · [Changes since v0.2.0](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Switchyard/compare/v0.2.0...v0.3.0)

## Routing and integrations

- Advisor Gate lets an executor model work with a stronger advisor for review, approval, and redo decisions, with session review budgets and stall checkpoints.
- Composite routing combines an LLM classifier with Stage Router. Auto presets provide capable and efficient Stage configurations.
- The new `switchyard-runner` crate loads TOML deployments and runs routing in-process. NeMo Relay and LiteLLM integrations use the native routing path.
- Sub-agent routing, per-target system prompts and reasoning effort, and per-client request deadlines provide more control over agent traffic

releases.name: v0.2.0
releases.body:
# Switchyard v0.2.0

Switchyard v0.2.0 is a substantial redesign of the project around a native Rust server and the new libsy library architecture. Across [193 commits](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Switchyard/compare/v0.1.0...v0.2.0), this release separates orchestration, provider-neutral protocols, translation, model transport, and serving into focused components that can be used together or embedded independently.

Switchyard remains pre-alpha software. APIs and configuration may change before a stable release.

## libsy Redesign

`switchyard-libsy` provides a provider-neutral framework for multi-LLM orchestration. Its `Algorithm` abstraction decides which semantic model targets to call, in what order, and how to combine their results.

Algorithms do not own provider SDKs or an HTTP stack. They yield model-call steps back to their host, allowing the same algorithm to run inside the Switchyard server, another proxy, an agent runtime, or an application with custom model clients. The driver supports both buffered and streaming execution, concurrent model calls, routing decisions, request processors, classifiers, and session-scoped state.

The redesign establishes clear crate bound

releases.name: v0.1.0
releases.body:
# Switchyard v0.1.0

Switchyard v0.1.0 was the first public release. It introduced the Python proxy, OpenAI and Anthropic format translation, YAML route bundles, initial routing strategies, coding-agent launchers, and request metrics.

This release is retained for historical reference. New users should start with v0.2.0.

- [nemo-switchyard 0.1.0 on PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/nemo-switchyard/0.1.0/)
- [Full v0.1.0 changelog](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Switchyard/blob/v0.1.0/CHANGELOG.md)

aiSummary.oneLiner: A fast Rust proxy and routing library for transparently translating and directing LLM traffic.
aiSummary.whatItDoes: Switchyard acts as an intelligent intermediary layer that routes and translates requests between various Large Language Model APIs, such as OpenAI and Anthropic formats. It allows applications, like coding agents or custom software, to communicate using their native protocol while seamlessly routing the traffic to entirely different backends like vLLM, Ollama, or NVIDIA NIM. Beyond simple translation, it provides sophisticated routing algorithms—including A/B benchmarking, signal-driven stage routing, and LLM-as-classifier routing—while actively recording operational metrics for performance monitoring. Built in Rust, it ensures minimal latency overhead whether run as a standalone server, embedded library, or command-line launcher.
keyFeatures: Protocol Translation: seamlessly converts requests and responses between OpenAI Chat, Anthropic Messages, and OpenAI Responses formats.
Advanced Traffic Routing: supports complex routing algorithms including random distribution, signal-driven stages, and custom user-defined logic.
Operational Metrics Export: natively exposes Prometheus metrics detailing request counts, error rates, token usage, and routing latency.
Flexible Deployment Modes: can be utilized as a standalone proxy server, a command-line launcher for coding agents, or an embedded Rust library.
Multi-Backend Support: abstracts the complexity of connecting to diverse LLM providers and self-hosted inference engines like vLLM or Ollama.
High-Performance Core: developed in Rust to ensure the proxy adds negligible latency to the critical path of LLM requests.

useCases.title: Agent Protocol Adaptation
useCases.description: Used by developers to point coding agents expecting an Anthropic API towards open-source models running locally on Ollama.

useCases.title: A/B Model Benchmarking
useCases.description: Used by AI teams to silently split production traffic across multiple LLM providers to evaluate response quality and latency.

useCases.title: LLM Infrastructure Observability
useCases.description: Used by platform engineers to centralize token usage tracking and error monitoring across disparate AI backends via Prometheus.

useCases.title: Dynamic Request Routing
useCases.description: Used by application backends to route complex queries to expensive frontier models while directing simple queries to cheaper, local models based on classifiers.

aiSummary.whoIsItFor: Switchyard is built for AI platform engineers, backend developers, and AI researchers who need to manage, route, and monitor traffic across multiple LLM providers. It is specifically useful for teams building complex AI applications that require interoperability between different API standards or need to abstract away the underlying inference engines. Users should be comfortable configuring proxy servers or writing Rust code.
